goals: Know when the bootstrap is useful
why: The bootstrap gives uncertainty estimates for almost any statistic (median, ratio, model accuracy) without formulas. It is also the "bagging" inside random forests.
explain: You have one sample. Pretend it is the population: draw a new sample of the **same size with replacement** (some rows appear twice, some not at all) and compute your statistic.
Repeat thousands of times. The spread of those statistics approximates the sampling uncertainty.
A **percentile CI**: take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap statistics.
Great for medians, percentiles, ratios and custom business metrics where no simple formula exists.

example.title: Median delivery time
steps: Resample 50 times with replacement → median 37; again → 39; …
2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the medians: 35 and 41 min
example.result: 95% bootstrap CI for the median: 35–41 minutes, with no formula needed.

mistakes: Resampling without replacement (that just shuffles the data).
Bootstrapping very small samples (fewer than ~20) and trusting the result.
Ignoring dependence (time series need a block bootstrap).
takeaways: The spread of the results = uncertainty

practice.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.gamma(4, 10, 50)
meds = [np.median(rng.choice(x, len(x), replace=True)) for _ in range(10_000)]
print(round(np.median(x), 1), np.percentile(meds, [2.5, 97.5]).round(1))
